title: Counting — numbers and counter words
goal: Count from one to a hundred, and use the counter words -টা and -জন — something English has only in phrases like “a piece of” or “three head of cattle”, but Bengali uses with every number.
bekal: count ১ to ২০ and the tens up to ১০০
attach -টা for things and -জন for people
ask কয়টা (how many things) and কতজন (how many people)
understand লাখ and কোটি, which English does not use

dialogs.title: কথোপকথন — At the sweet shop
dialogs.intro: Mitali takes Ani along to buy মিষ্টি — Bengali sweets — for this afternoon's guests. Notice that every number gets a small ending stuck to it before the thing is named: that is the counter word.

lines.speaker: দোকানদার:
lines.id: Yes, sister, what will you need?

lines.speaker: মিতালি:
lines.id: Give me ten rosogolla, and five sandesh.
lines.literal: ten-(things) — rosogolla — give, and — five-(things) — sandesh.

lines.speaker: দোকানদার:
lines.id: Sure. How many guests at home?

lines.speaker: মিতালি:
lines.id: Six. And there are four of us.

lines.speaker: আনি:
lines.id: Mitali, how many are in here?

lines.speaker: মিতালি:
lines.id: That box has twelve. One dozen.
lines.literal: that — box-in — twelve-(things) — exist. one — dozen.

lines.speaker: আনি:
lines.id: I'll take three. I'll eat them in my room.

lines.speaker: দোকানদার:
lines.id: Eighteen altogether. Two hundred seventy taka.
lines.literal: all — together — eighteen-(things). two-hundred — seventy — taka.

lines.speaker: আনি:
lines.id: Two hundred seventy? Please say it a bit more slowly!

lines.speaker: দোকানদার:
lines.id: Ha ha! Two hun-dred se-ven-ty. Here, I'll write it on paper — 270.
lines.literal: ha ha! two-hundred-seventy. this — here, paper-on — writing — am-giving — 270.

lines.speaker: আনি:
lines.id: Thank you! I'm learning Bengali numbers too.

lines.speaker: দোকানদার:
lines.id: Very good! Then one more, free.
lines.literal: very — good! then — more — one-(thing) — free.

notes: **A number never stands directly before a noun — there is always an ending in between.** You can't say *তিন বই*; the correct form is **তিনটা বই** (three books). That ending is called a counter word. English has a faint echo of it — *three **pieces** of cake*, *two **head** of cattle*, *a **sheet** of paper* — but in Bengali it is required with every number. It feels odd for a week, then becomes automatic.

**Two endings cover ninety percent of your needs: -টা for things, -জন for people.** একটা বই (a book), দুটো আম (two mangoes), তিনজন ছাত্র (three students), কতজন? (how many people?). ⚠️ **Never** use -টা for people — একটা লোক sounds like you are talking about a person as an object.

⚠️ **Some number + ending combinations change shape and must be learned as new words.** এক + টা = **একটা**; দুই + টা = **দুটো** (not *দুইটা*); দুই + জন = **দুজন** (not *দুইজন*); তিন + টা = **তিনটে · তিনটা**. From four on, the combinations become regular again: চারটা, পাঁচটা, ছয়টা.

**Every number from one to a hundred is its own word — and there is no shortcut.** Unlike English, which builds “twenty-three” from two pieces, Bengali has a single word for each number: ২১ **একুশ**, ২২ **বাইশ**, ২৩ **তেইশ**. ⚠️ The good news: at A1 you **only need ১–২০ and the tens**; the rest you can guess from resemblance, and people will understand বিশ-তিন if you hold up your fingers.

⚠️ **লাখ and কোটি — two units English does not use.** After হাজার (thousand), Bengali doesn't jump to “million” but to **লাখ** *lakh* = **one hundred thousand**, then **কোটি** *koTi* = **ten million**. So a house price is “thirty lakh” (3,000,000), not “three million”. If you hear a number that sounds impossible, the unit is probably different, not the price.

**Bengali digits are still alive on the street.** Bus numbers, prices on market boards, house numbers and page numbers are often written ০ ১ ২ ৩ ৪ ৫ ৬ ৭ ৮ ৯. There are only ten, and some look like digits you know — ২ looks like a backwards 2, ৪ like an unfinished 8. One afternoon of memorizing is enough, and it pays off at once.

**একটু আস্তে বলুন — the lifesaver for numbers.** Numbers are the fastest-spoken part of any language. Don't be shy about asking for a repeat, or asking for it in writing: **লিখে দিন** (*li-khé din* — please write it down). Any shopkeeper will gladly do it, and a phone calculator is a perfectly legitimate friend.

after: ⚠️ **আশি (80) and আশা (hope) differ by just one letter** — look carefully. Likewise **নয়** meaning “nine” and **নয়** meaning “is not”: two words written exactly the same, told apart only by their place in the sentence.

grammars.title: Counter words
after: **কত** *kôt* on its own means “how much” and is used for uncountable things — কত টাকা? (how much money?), কত দূর? (how far?). For countable things, add the ending: **কয়টা** (how many things), **কতজন** (how many people).

blocks.title: Bengali sweets — and counting them
items: **রসগোল্লা** *rôshgôlla* — round cheese balls in sugar syrup, spongy and moist. Bengal's pride, fought over by Bangladesh and West Bengal all the way to a geographical-indication court case.
**সন্দেশ** *sôndésh* — a firm cheese sweet, drier and finer; usually sold by the piece and boxed as a gift.
**মিষ্টি দই** *mishTi dôi* — sweet yogurt in a clay pot. ⚠️ This is no ordinary dessert; refusing it in someone's home can feel like refusing the host's hospitality.
**Bringing মিষ্টি when you visit is a custom, not a luxury.** One small box is enough, and your host will count it in front of you — so the numbers in this unit get used right away.

blocks.text: A note on money. The currency of Bangladesh is the **টাকা** *Taka*, and in everyday Bengali India's currency is also called **টাকা**, even though its official name is the rupee. The word **পয়সা** *pôysa* means a small coin, but in conversation it more often means “money” in general — like saying *cash*. If someone asks **পয়সা আছে?**, they are asking whether you have money on you, not whether you have coins.

exercises.prompt: Write these numbers as Bengali words.
Put the words in the right order.

items: There are two chairs in the room.

answers: তিন — সাত — বারো — বিশ — পঞ্চাশ — একশো
টেবিলে দুটো বই আছে। — আপনাদের পরিবারে কতজন? — দুকাপ চা দিন। — এটার দাম কত? — আমি দশ দিন থাকব।
কতজন অতিথি? — দশটা রসগোল্লা দিন। — আমার বয়স পঁচিশ। — ঘরে দুটো চেয়ার আছে। — এটার দাম কত? — আমরা চারজন।
